title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
description: SpaceX hit profitability in the third quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
content: SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income. CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing . That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition. The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company. The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter. During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online. “People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.” In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly. Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages. SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity. Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million. Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.” More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion. title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
description: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built using its technology, citing national security concerns.
content: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security . The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said. The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an offic i al briefing . “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
description: Eka Robotics may be the first robotic arm that is actually good at picking up a wide range of objects, and it is so smooth and human-like, it is wowing the industry.
content: Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime. “They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch. In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.” Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to 10 years ago. Take a look for yourself: Loading the player… What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?” When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch. How not to squish the raspberry These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks , say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point. “Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.” Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. “Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.” Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California–Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gig workers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them. “What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues. Making a general-purpose robot useful Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models — the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks — aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones. The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it. “Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.” Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real. “What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.” Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms. “What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.” Topics AI , Exclusive , Robotics When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol
description: Figma said it plans to support as many standards as possible without exposing all of its data.
content: Despite Figma co-founder Dylan Field’s concerns about MCP (model context protocol), which standardizes how AI agents connect to external data sources and tools, the company is expanding its support for the open source standard. At the design company’s first Config conference held in India, the company announced 20 new MCP partners, including Amp, ClickUp, Dia, Junie by JetBrains, Linear, Meta Muse, Mistral, Notion, OpenCode, and Sarvam Agents. Field has expressed his misgivings about MCP before. Days before this announcement, one of MCP’s co-creators complained about Figma not supporting the open source tool Pi. As part of his response, Field made a comment about Anthropic not making its various resources available via MCP. “I find it interesting that Anthropic (creators of MCP standard) do not expose artifacts/other cloud resources created via MCP,” he wrote on X. “The debate is framed as open vs closed. Everyone always prefers open … obviously. And meanwhile issues of asymmetric context sharing are ignored.” (Field later added that Figma plans support Pi. ) Can you help me understand why you don't make various Anthropic resources available via MCP? Maybe I'm missing something. — Dylan Field (@zoink) September 30, 2026 At a media briefing, I asked Field about this debate. The co-founder explained that while Figma wants to be open, he doesn’t think MCP is a perfect protocol. “I’m really excited about what we’re doing in terms of opening up our ecosystem. I also think that MCP is not a perfect protocol. And I think that it is something that has tons of room for improvement,” the co-founder responded. “It is advantaged more to frontier labs. Also, I understand everyone online who just wants a protocol that they can use when they want to use their Figma data, and I want them to use it, too.” Figma’s CEO said that the reason the company doesn’t want to be fully open is that the more data the company exposes through MCP, the higher the chance of abuse. He also clarified that while most users don’t intend to use MCP or Figma data in a malicious way, the company still has to think about those potential risks. content: Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation. The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data. Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) . The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures. The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn. “Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.” There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola , and Read AI ; new entrants like Calendly , Wispr , and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom ; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill. Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant , a search function that works across apps , and integration with other AI tools . Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings. “When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said. The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge. content: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. Electric Plant co-founders Lee von Kraus (right) and Justin Mast stand next to a tree with a sensor attached to it. Image Credits: Electric Plant The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” Topics AI , Climate , Exclusive , Fundraising , plant monitoring , plants When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code Today we’re introducing FairStress , a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into Olmo-eval , our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations. Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant? Arriving at the same answer in two versions of a scenario can hide meaningful differences in how readily a model changes that decision when challenged, however. Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other. FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries. Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call adversarial prefixes – can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing. With FairStress, our target is symmetric fairness —when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits. FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness. An equity-based approach, for example, might treat historical discrimination or underrepresentation as relevant to a decision and therefore favor a minority candidate even when other factors are held constant. Measuring fairness beyond the final answer FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication. Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other. FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly. Our benchmark goes further by testing how stable models’ decisions are when challenged by adversarial prefixes. These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports. Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases. Alongside the full benchmark, we’ve developed FairStress-Core, a 50K-item subset selected using item response theory, following our Fluid Benchmarking approach. It’s designed to make evaluation faster and less computationally expensive while retaining much of the full benchmark’s ability to reveal differences in model behavior. Models do not always hold correct answers equally In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric. For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one. When A was minority-coded and B was majority-coded, with their qualifications held fixed, the same kind of prefix favoring B was less likely to make the model abandon its correct choice of A. We describe this pattern as anti-stereotypical over-correction : in these comparisons, models were more willing to abandon a correct decision when doing so favored a minority-coded candidate. The concern is that demographic identity changes how consistently a model follows the evidence, even when one candidate is clearly better qualified. In this hiring example, Tülu 3.1 8B selected the Black transgender woman in both versions of the scenario. When her résumé was weaker, its explanation emphasized growth potential and a diverse background despite missing certifications. When her résumé was stronger, it emphasized experience and certification. Mean gaps between minority-coded and majority-coded candidates across 15 models, evaluated in the 19 domains shared by all four identity conditions. Values are in percentage points. Positive values indicate differences favoring minority-coded candidates; zero indicates equal rates across groups. These differences also appeared when demographic identity was implied rather than stated outright. Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.9 percentage points with implied identity and 9.3 points with explicit labels. On FairStress-Core, frontier models including Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.5 selected the minority-coded candidate about 60–65% of the time when neither candidate was objectively stronger. Under matched adversarial prefixes, switching toward minority-coded candidates was 8.8–42.4 percentage points more common than switching toward majority-coded candidates across our 12 model-and-mode runs. We found subtler differences in how models explained their choices, even when they chose correctly in both demographic versions of a scenario. Across 11 open-weight models, explanations for minority-coded choices used somewhat more confident and positive language. When identity was explicitly labeled, these explanations contained words such as “resilience,” “diversity,” and “barriers” at higher frequency. Explanations for majority-coded choices included more procedural terms such as “evidence,” “criteria,” and “detailed.” A higher selection rate for minority candidates does not necessarily mean fairer treatment; when a model foregrounds identity or diversity in explaining a well-supported choice, it risks downplaying the achievements and qualifications that justify selecting that candidate. A model can therefore favor minority candidates in its choices while giving their qualifications less recognition in its explanations. In a controlled analysis of Gemma-3-12B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, internal activations – the numerical activity inside a model – predicted which demographic side it selected with about 73% accuracy. Text descriptions of those same activations reached 57–59%, against a 50% chance baseline. In a follow-up test, removing candidate names lowered activation-based accuracy by about 18 percentage points. Our activation analysis is limited to two models and only a handful of demographic contrasts, so we treat these findings as narrower than the broader behavioral results. Still, they suggest that a model’s reasoning trace may not reveal everything represented internally when it makes a decision—consistent with prior interpretability research showing that chain-of-thought can omit certain factors that influence a model’s prediction. Why existing benchmarks can produce a different result We also wanted to understand how FairStress compares with existing measures of demographic bias in LLMs. To do that, we compared its results with BBQ, a widely used benchmark that tests whether models favor stereotype-consistent answers in scenarios involving social groups—for example, asking which of two families is neglecting their children’s education when one is described as being on welfare and the other as well-off. In our BBQ evaluation, models generally leaned toward stereotype-consistent answers, while FairStress revealed a tendency to favor minority-coded candidates. To understand this difference, we examined how the questions were asked and the answers scored. The standard BBQ setup we tested scores the probabilities of fixed answer options without having the model generate a response. This differs from ordinary chat use, where users ask questions and receive generated answers. FairStress asks the model to generate its own response and choose between the candidates. To see whether the evaluation setup explained the discrepancy between FairStress and BBQ, we took the same BBQ questions and model weights and tested five configurations that varied the chat template, question wording, and use of fixed-option probability scoring or answer generation. In this controlled comparison, we tested Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. With a chat template, yes/no wording, and generated answers, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct shifted from stereotype-consistent to minority-favoring behavior, while Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct moved to roughly neutral—suggesting that the direction of measured bias depends partly on how a benchmark asks the question and scores the answer. Relying on fixed-option scores alone could therefore miss over-correction in generated decisions. Evaluating both would give developers a fuller picture of the behavior their fairness interventions need to address. Training for symmetric robustness To investigate possible sources of the asymmetry, we audited data from Olmo 3’s training pipeline. Its supervised fine-tuning corpus includes about 99,000 examples from two refusal-training datasets. Across 28,000 topic clusters in the fine-tuning and preference-training data, we found only nine clusters discussing decisions based on merit rather than demographics—and all nine consisted of refusals. The audit also found unequal portrayals of demographic groups: minority-coded groups received more protective or positive framing, while white and cisgender people received little protective framing and persistent negative framing. Together, these findings suggest a gap between teaching models to refuse discriminatory requests and showing them how to make decisions on merit. Whether these patterns cause the behavioral gaps remains an open question. Net framing of seven demographic groups across Olmo 3’s training data. Each value is the percentage of passages classified as positive toward a group minus the percentage classified as negative. The preference-tuning column covers only the preferred responses, and the reinforcement-learning column covers only prompts. Some reinforcement-learning estimates are based on small samples—as few as eight prompts—and should be interpreted cautiously. Can existing fixes help? FairStress can also be used to evaluate whether debiasing techniques actually produce more robust, fairer model behavior. We tested nine interventions, including self-critique (where the model reviews and revises its own answer), activation steering (which directly shifts internal model representations during generation), and learned edits (small, targeted changes to internal model representations that are learned from examples). Most methods did not reliably reduce the asymmetry, and some produced more balanced choices at a substantial cost to accuracy. For example, one activation-steering method reduced Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s accuracy on clear-cut decisions from 98% to 47%. One approach came closer to symmetric robustness: counterfactual chain-of-thought, which asks the model to reconsider a case with the candidates’ demographic identities swapped. Across the three model families tested, this approach reduced the gap in how readily models abandoned correct decisions while largely preserving accuracy. It did not remove every asymmetry; on ambiguous cases, models still favored minority-coded candidates. From fair outcomes to fair decision-making FairStress shows why a model’s demographic fairness can’t be judged solely by whether it reaches the same final choice across otherwise equivalent scenarios. A model can select the candidate best supported by the evidence in two versions of the same scenario that differ only in demographic identity, yet be easier to sway in one version, explain its choice differently, or show different internal activation patterns. Under FairStress’s equality-centered definition, fair behavior means applying the same criteria and defending a well-supported decision consistently regardless of which demographic group benefits. More broadly, this work reflects our goal of building evaluations that better capture how models behave in real-world settings. By releasing FairStress, we hope researchers and model builders can use it to diagnose hidden asymmetries, test proposed fixes, and develop training approaches that produce more consistent and trustworthy results. Open, rigorous evaluation is central to our broader work at Ai2, and we hope FairStress gives the community another useful tool for understanding where models fall short and how to improve them. Meta says it paused a Muse feature that lets you share conversations with the AI assistant after researchers found the URLs publicly available on the web, as reported by Ars Technica . In a report published this week , researchers at the security firm Claroc say they found more than 6,800 Muse links through public DNS records. “People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link,” Muse spokesperson Tracy Clayton says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.” The feature in question allows you to share your Muse conversation with someone else through a link. But, as pointed out by Claroc, the way Meta designed these links made them easy to find. “Muse builds each share’s web address from the share’s title, a short phrase describing the conversation, then a random ID,” Claroc says. “The hostname usually gave away what a page held before we opened it, and since the link carries that same title and ID, a hostname pulled from DNS rebuilds the link.” Related Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents By searching public DNS records, which serve as a directory for web traffic, Claroc was able to view hundreds of Muse conversations, including some containing a marketing company’s revenue review, a small business owner’s loan application, a workplace’s full-year staff calendar, and notes for a job candidate’s call with an AI lab. This isn’t the first time AI sharing features made chats more public than intended, as conversations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT , Anthropic’s Claude , and xAI’s Grok have wound up on Google Search. title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
description: Google has joined Amazon in releasing a developer tool that makes it easy for PyTorch users to move their apps off Nvidia GPUs.
content: On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs. PyTorch is the popular open source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects. Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no rewriting of their apps. Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it’s going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default. Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM), RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does. Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops, and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps. None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage. Topics AI , Google , Hardware When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
description: Meta's AI companion Muse has surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days, joining an exclusive group of apps that includes Threads. New data also shows Muse is retaining users at higher rates than its AI rivals.
content: Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States. Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023. Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other non-game app to make it into the exclusive club. Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse. Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September. Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data. Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase. Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days. Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.) Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. title: The new economics of enterprise AI
description: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?” Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models: A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change. On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action. An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn’t free inference; it’s control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management. The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system. Ownership is an operating discipline Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn’t make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way. One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive. The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn’t a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it’s a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness. Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment. From deployment to value HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload’s requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices. In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization. Measure what matters Token consumption remains useful, but it isn’t a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity. Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck. For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn’t whether enterprises will pay for AI — it’s whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it. title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
description: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
content: Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution. Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53 , which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.” Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes. It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes. Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework , which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said. The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death , the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking . A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls. In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions. Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse. Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all . title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: ‘Physical AI is in its LEGO era’
description: It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity.
content: It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity. She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex. Listen on Apple Podcasts Listen on Spotify She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords. “A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.” “There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued. Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now, too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced. “We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.” “Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space. “This just makes it a lot easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said. title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Mattt mattt Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> MPS in PyTorch 2.15 Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 Irakli Salia Isalia20 Follow Khushi Agrawal khushi-411 Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads. A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors. TL;DR FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU! MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing. Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster. More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition. Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB. More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing. Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later ; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later . A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding. What this means for you If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice: Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ( More ) Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ( More ) Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ( reported in ComfyUI ). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB. FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. ( More ) Contents Getting started FP8 comes to MPS Faster language-model decoding Linear algebra gets a boost Convolutions, padding, and training Softmax and reductions A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding More control with MPS streams More operations work on MPS A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Wrapping up Getting started You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix ). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why. To try the release candidate in a separate environment: uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu FP8 comes to MPS FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16. You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm , which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def quantize_fp8 ( x ): limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn). max scale = x. abs ().amax().clamp_min( 1e-12 ) / limit return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale x = torch.randn( 1 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32) weight = torch.randn( 1024 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32) x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x) w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight) y = F.scaled_mm( x_fp8, w_fp8.t(), scale_a=x_scale, scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, scale_b=w_scale, scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, output_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) print (y.shape, y.dtype) Faster language-model decoding Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers. Linear layers MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear , so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup . The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×. Mixture-of-experts layers A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation . In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well. For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F tokens = torch.randn( 64 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16) weights = torch.randn( 3 , 128 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16) ends = torch.tensor([ 16 , 48 , 64 ], device= "mps" , dtype=torch.int32) out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(- 2 , - 1 ), offs=ends) print (out.shape) # torch.Size([64, 128]) The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second : Linear algebra gets a boost Complex-valued computations Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization , LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU: import torch a = torch.randn( 8 , 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) a = a + 8 * torch.eye( 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) b = torch.randn( 8 , 2 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a) x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b) print ((a @ x - b). abs (). max ().item()) Small matrices and larger solves Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates , and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication. Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides. SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values , very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True , which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable. Convolutions, padding, and training Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal: Operation What changes in 2.15 conv1d forward Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes. Constant padding Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below). Reflection and replication padding New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness. Out-of-place dropout nn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel. Upsampling backward A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path. Channels-last conv2d backward Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access. Softmax and reductions Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs , about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes: A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB : Memory metric MPSGraph padding Metal padding Current tensor-allocation peak 4.422 GiB 4.095 GiB Allocator-reserved peak 8.070 GiB 8.070 GiB Total driver-memory peak 270.135 GiB 8.108 GiB More control with MPS streams You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream. Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result: import torch x = torch.randn( 1024 , device= "mps" ) torch.mps.synchronize() worker = torch.mps.Stream() with torch.mps.stream(worker): y = x.square() x.record_stream(worker) del x worker.synchronize() print (y.cpu().shape) More operations work on MPS Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp , torch.logspace , torch.take and Tensor.put_ , torch.heaviside , torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons . logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element. Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly . A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release. Faster LLM decoding Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels , so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context: Model Before After Change LFM2.5-8B-A1B 108.8 tokens/s 126.0 tokens/s +16% Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 52.9 tokens/s 62.8 tokens/s +19% Qwen3.8-27B 12.1 tokens/s 12.6 tokens/s +4% Attention runs entirely on Metal Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely : every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms. More MPSGraph to Metal migrations The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond. A smaller install Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default , with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication. Wrapping up PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try! What's next for us More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph. torch.compile : we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end. Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.
