description: Anthropic is reportedly struggling to secure enough compute from cloud providers that increasingly view it as a competitor, even as its infrastructure spending balloons ahead of a planned November IPO.
content: In Brief Posted: 2:25 PM PDT · October 20, 2026 Image Credits: Getty Images Rebecca Bellan Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal . The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation. And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers. Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant
description: Yelp is embedding numerous new AI features into its app that can do everything from call to check on restaurant wait times to create personalized recommendations that remember your preferences.
content: Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times. The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant. Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers . With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation. Image Credits: Yelp The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app. Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon. Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine; reorder; add notes to items; and share them with others. Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view. Image Credits: Yelp To cap off all these changes, Yelp has been thinking about enhancing customer support and business processes through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries . content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation Enterprise + Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 4 Lukas Zbinden lzbinden Follow nvidia Javier Gamazo javirk1 Follow nvidia Nigel Nelson nigeln Follow nvidia Mostafa Toloui mtoloui Follow nvidia Sean Huver shuver Follow nvidia :last-child]:mb-0"> Picture moving the Cadiere grasper, grasping the gallbladder, and lifting it, all within a generated surgical scene that responds in real time. Today, we take the next step and introduce Cosmos3-H-Dreams, bringing interactive generative simulation to the visual and procedural complexity of clinical surgery with our most convincing in-body imagery to date. Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism. Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. 1. From Tabletop Tasks to Clinical Scenes In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential. Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment. Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion. 2. What is New in Cosmos3-H-Dreams? 2.1 A Cosmos 3 Foundation and Richer Surgical Controls Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano , a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment , and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction. The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput. 2.2 From Teacher to Four-Step and Two-Step Students Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams. We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics. Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive. Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Self-Forcing then trains it on its own generated context, guided by the teacher and a learned critic. This helps address the accumulation of errors during interactive rollouts. The first released student uses four denoising steps per generated block. We then train that student further with a two-step schedule to produce the second release checkpoint. The two-step model is separately trained, not simply the four-step model run with fewer sampling steps. Fewer denoising steps results in faster inference time at the expense of lower visual quality. Both checkpoints let developers explore the balance between visual quality and inference cost. 2.3 Streaming through FlashDreams FlashDreams supplies the accelerated streaming runtime. Long rollouts also require managing the model’s attention history. The Cosmos3-H-Dreams integration uses an adapted FadeMem module that consolidates the growing key/value cache during long rollouts. This complements Self-Forcing: distillation addresses how the model learns from its generated history, while cache consolidation addresses how that history is stored during streaming generation. 3. Exploring Unseen Trajectories During a clinical procedure there may be complications or some room for the surgeon to perform “novel” movements. Therefore, a simulator must be able to generalize beyond the training data, and produce coherent frames with unseen movements. The demonstrations below show Cosmos3-H-Dreams generating different cholecystectomy scenes conditioned on instrument actions recorded with a VR headset. The two videos begin with the same initial frame but follow different action sequences illustrating how instrument control leads to distinct continuations of the same scene with physically accurate tissue deformations. Furthermore, these rollouts allow us to inspect whether instruments follow the controls, whether tissue responds coherently to interaction, and whether anatomical and instrument appearance remain consistent over time. 4. Adapting to Your Own Data and Controller Cosmos3-H-Dreams includes four-step and two-step checkpoints for cholecystectomy. The system can be adapted to other datasets and embodiments with synchronized video and compatible action representations. To train a real-time student model on your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and Self-Forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide . It describes data preparation, public teacher-training tools, and the distillation stages. Controller integrations must use the same action conventions and normalization as training. 5. What is Next The advance in visual realism opens several research directions: Model the full procedure. Expand coverage and temporal consistency so all phases of cholecystectomy can be explored systematically, with clear task boundaries and success criteria. Connect generative and numerical simulation. Combine learned visual realism with explicit geometry, contact and tissue mechanics. Numerical models and measured data could help constrain and validate deformation, making simulation behavior inspectable as well as convincing. Evaluate with surgeons. Assess anatomical accuracy, instrument behavior and tissue response, turning expert feedback into reproducible benchmarks. Support more instruments. Move beyond two controlled tools to richer coordination, occlusion and interaction. Develop autonomous surgical policies. Couple world action models to Cosmos3-H-Dreams in a closed loop, so policies can learn defined cholecystectomy subtasks. These are research directions, not established clinical capabilities. Cosmos3-H-Dreams is a research simulator, not a validated system for patient care. It offers a foundation for studying surgical interaction in an increasingly realistic environment. 6. We look forward to seeing what the community builds inside these new surgical worlds. title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
description: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie. The AI adoption spectrum by industry Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1). Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing. Source : TripleTen , 2026 While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge. By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers. The AI skills workers are being asked to learn Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn’t previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2). Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting. One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like. How early AI adoption helps your career Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice. In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth. Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn’t matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren’t boxed in by them anymore.” The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry: Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0) Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0) Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0) Education: $883 average (42% spent $0) Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3). Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills. However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%). Conclusion The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations. title: ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 23 +17 Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan ashwath-vaithina Follow ibm-research Vatche Isahagian Vatche Follow ibm-research Vinod Muthusamy vinodmut Follow ibm-research Jayaram Radhakrishnan jayaramkr Follow ibm-research Evelyn Duesterwald evduester Follow ibm-research Gaodan Fang gaodan-fang Follow ibm-research Punleuk Oum illeatmyhat Follow ibm-research G Thomas gsthomasx Follow ibm-research Michał Ulewicz Michal Follow ibm-research Merve Unuvar mrvnvr Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research :last-child]:mb-0"> ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights. Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt. ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed. Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions. τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline . We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list: You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below. Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed. <policy> # Retail agent policy As a retail agent, you can help users: - cancel or modify pending orders - return or exchange delivered orders - modify their default user address … </policy> ## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully): - Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. If email is unavailable, verify identity via full name and zip code using the find_user_id_by_name_zip API. - Always confirm all intended changes (modify, cancel, return, exchange) with a clear, structured summary, and require explicit user approval before executing any database-updating action. - When processing a return or exchange, communicate the refund with an itemized breakdown and clarify refund timing — don't wait for the user to ask. - Take one action per step: never combine a tool call with a user-facing message in the same turn, and wait for the tool's result before replying. - Before looking a user up, parse and clean their name — e.g. split a combined handle like `daiki_johnson_9523` into first/last name — and after a couple of failed lookups, state the exact format you need. … We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using gpt-4.1 , the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set. Guidelines improve capability and reliability In a prior post , we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model. Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1). Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain. Variant Guidelines included in context Retail Airline baseline no guidelines 0 0 sup3 support n ≥ 3 (high-support core) 31 14 lossless all guidelines 292 101 The metrics we track. Every task is attempted 4 times , and we read those trials two ways: Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right? Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average. Figure 1. Mean Accuracy and Pass^4 on held-out retail and airline tasks for agents using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Agent model: gpt-4.1 (user simulator: gpt-5.5 ). Table 2. Held-out agent performance using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Parentheses show percentage-point changes from baseline. Domain (test tasks) Config Mean Accuracy Pass^4 Retail (40) baseline 78.1% 57.5% sup3 78.8% (+0.7) 60.0% (+2.5) lossless 82.5% (+4.4) 67.5% (+10.0) Airline (20) baseline 57.5% 35.0% sup3 60.0% (+2.5) 45.0% (+10.0) lossless 65.0% (+7.5) 40.0% (+5.0) Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below. The best amount of guidance depends on the domain The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail , more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant , support count is a knob worth tuning per domain , not a value to hard-code. Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns Guidelines aren't free, but the cost lands where you'd expect — in prompt input tokens , not in a longer, more meandering conversation: Figure 2. Total LLM cost per conversation by domain and guideline configuration on the full base split. Table 3. Total LLM cost per conversation (agent and user simulator) on the full base split across four trials. Lower is better. Domain Config Cost / conversation vs. baseline Retail baseline $0.084 — sup3 $0.095 +12% lossless $0.139 +65% Airline baseline $0.081 — sup3 $0.097 +19% lossless $0.107 +32% Does the agent get there by talking longer ? To answer that cleanly we compare like for like : the task runs solved under both baseline and the guideline variant — identical scenario and seed, a true "same task, done right" set — and count assistant turns on each side. Table 4. Assistant turns per conversation for matched runs solved under both settings on the test split, pooling four trials. Domain Shared set Solved under both (n) Baseline turns +Guidelines Δ Retail baseline ∩ sup3 108 10.40 10.35 −0.05 baseline ∩ lossless 111 10.59 10.16 −0.43 Airline baseline ∩ sup3 38 8.97 8.53 −0.45 baseline ∩ lossless 40 9.15 8.82 −0.33 The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter : lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching , since the guideline block is identical across every call. So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together. Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — gpt-4.1 . A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using gpt-5.5 for both the agent and guideline extraction , on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3. Table 5. Held-out airline performance for the gpt-5.5 agent across four trials per task. Airline · gpt-5.5 (20 held-out test tasks) Accuracy Pass^4 baseline (0 guidelines) 72.5% 55.0% sup2 (103 guidelines) 80.0% (+7.5) 70.0% (+15.0) lossless (146 guidelines) 82.5% (+10.0) 70.0% (+15.0) The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with gpt-4.1 on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw. ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4 . Because that covers the full task set rather than the held-out test split, these figures differ from the test-task numbers reported above. This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into , or past , current frontier company: Retail: #1 . On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5% , ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data . Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points . Airline: #1 using gpt-5.5 , #8 using gpt-4.1 Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using gpt-4.1 Pass^4 = 44% — 8th , beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using gpt-5.5 reaches 82.0% , clearing every frontier entry (66–72%). Figure 3. Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026. Same message in both domains: learning guidelines around the model works across different base models — bringing an agent using an older, non-reasoning model into frontier company on retail, and taking an agent using a frontier model to the top on airline. Agents can improve without weight updates Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs , automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage. Image: Adobe Andrew Liszewski is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid. Adobe announced yesterday that the mobile version of Lightroom , available for iOS, iPadOS, and Android, can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI with just a single tap. When the app detects a person, or a group of people, have their eyes closed in a photo it will automatically present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action that appears as an icon over the image providing easy access to the new feature. Being able to easily save an otherwise great photo by opening a subject’s eyes has been a feature in Adobe’s Photoshop Elements for nearly a decade, but as DPReview points out , Elements sources the replacement from another photo of the subject with mixed results depending on variations between the two images. Open Eyes in Lightroom mobile instead relies on generative AI so the replacement eyes match the lighting and pose, and the app will use other images of the same person in your Lightroom library as reference so the open eyes will accurately match the color, size, and shape of their own. Image: Adobe You can perform a similar fix in other Adobe apps like Photoshop using its own generative AI tools, but it’s not a one-tap fix, and it’s not free. Those using the free version of the Lightroom mobile app can try the Open Eyes feature twice before they’re given a prompt to subscribe to an Adobe Creative Cloud plan that includes more credits for its various AI-powered tools, according to DPReview . title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M US downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
description: New data also shows Muse is retaining users at higher rates than its AI rivals.
content: Meta’s AI companion , Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower , Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States. Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s senior insights analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023. Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other nongame app to make it into the exclusive club. Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse. Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September. Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data. Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase. Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store and at one point even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days. Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.) Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days. Topics AI , Apps , Meta , muse When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Monday night that New Yorkers must resist the narrative that an AI takeover is inevitable and demand regulations that protect the public and put power back in their hands.
content: Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society. Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity and to take back control instead. His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute , a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable. Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her. “It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though … this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said. Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings. Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives. “Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.” He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children . Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack. “There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,” he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.” Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027. Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI. “At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said. President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force , announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction. “As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said. content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 19 +13 Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow Régis Pierrard regisss Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla , or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU , a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu" , and you're done. Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔 TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit . TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini. TPUs are available on Google Cloud , from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale. The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in. The old way Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA ( torch_xla ). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about. To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers. Enter TorchTPU 🚀 TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command: pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch . Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU. Your favourite libraries, now on TPU Transformers Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu" . That's it. from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "tpu" , # will load model directly on the TPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) inputs = tokenizer( "The future of AI is" , return_tensors= "pt" ).to( "tpu" ) out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 64 ) print (tokenizer.decode(out[ 0 ], skip_special_tokens= True )) The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup. Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨 TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu") . For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain. import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium" , dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) pipe.to( "tpu" ) # eager mode: that's the whole change # optional: compiled mode pipe.transformer. compile (backend= "tpu" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) image = pipe( "a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon" ).images[ 0 ] The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph. Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe. Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4: TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1 MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1 "The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager "A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps Kernels The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost. TPU kernels are written in Pallas , which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model: from kernels import get_kernel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu" kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version= 1 , trust_remote_code=[repo_id]) ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register( "tokamax_ragged_dot" , kernel.experts_forward) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507" , experts_implementation= "tokamax_ragged_dot" , ) The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B. Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation. We test it so you don't have to 🧪 We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[ https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard] . The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress! It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream. If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do. Get started TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu" . title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
description: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

content: Tech AI News Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive. Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive. by Emma Roth Oct 20, 2026, 10:11 PM UTC Image: Google Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April . Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months. content: In Brief Posted: 1:35 PM PDT · October 20, 2026 Image Credits: FotografiaBasica (opens in a new window) / Getty Images Julie Bort OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced on its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC. Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug-discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials. OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠. The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out. Spotify has also made changes to its music recommendation system to highlight songs from human artists. by Emma Roth Oct 20, 2026, 2:18 PM UTC Illustration by Nick Barclay / The Verge Part Of All the latest in AI ‘music’ see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Spotify says it has removed more than 50 million songs considered AI-generated slop or spam from user recommendations over the past year. That’s according to an announcement on Tuesday that says Spotify has also made changes to its recommendation system to highlight more music made by human artists. “Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” Spotify says. “Since we made these changes, we’ve seen a marked decrease in listener concerns about this content showing up in recommendations.” Though Spotify has stopped short of mandating labels on all AI tracks, it launched an “AI Persona” badge for artists that use an AI identity and don’t represent a real person. It also won’t recommend music from AI personas. Other music streaming platforms are taking a tougher stance on AI music, with YouTube Music putting labels on AI songs, Deezer giving users an option to filter out AI slop, and Bandcamp banning AI music entirely . Related AI music is flooding streaming services — but who wants it? Spotify says it uses a combination of listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and third-party AI detection tools to determine whether a track may be AI-generated slop. Last year, the company said it took down more than 75 million songs identified as spam . It’s also partnering with Universal Music Group and the independent music publisher Believe to launch a tool for creating AI music remixes . content: In Brief Posted: 10:55 AM PDT · October 20, 2026 Image Credits: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg / Getty Images Marina Temkin Eric Schmidt reportedly owns about half as much of Anthropic as CEO Dario Amodei Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger. The former Google CEO is reported to own about 1% of Anthropic after investing tens of millions of dollars in the leading AI lab’s Series A round in 2021, per Bloomberg. The startup was valued at $461 million at the time, according to PitchBook data. If Bloomberg’s estimate is accurate, Schmidt’s stake is remarkably large compared with the 2% of the company that co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei holds. Anthropic is widely expected to go public before the end of the year, with top-end market estimates valuing the company at as much as $2 trillion. At that valuation, Schmidt would add as much as $20 billion to his net worth, which Bloomberg currently puts at $57.5 billion. Schmidt has been an active tech investor since stepping down as Google CEO in 2011. He deploys capital through multiple entities, including Tomorrow Ventures, Innovation Endeavors Management, and his family office, Hillspire. His other AI bets include Mistral, General Intuition, and Reflection AI. Schmidt and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment. title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
description: The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
content: OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices. Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time. The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat. The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations . Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled. OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting. Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results. With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats. OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN. Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings. Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
description: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue," take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
content: Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown , take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents. “Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X . “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.” To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well , including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened. In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment and spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible. But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack. In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.” Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.” But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers. The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack. But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote. It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen. Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!” In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take. title: Otter AI raises $320M from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool
description: Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.
content: Meeting notetaking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation. The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data. Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) . The company said it’s now approaching new milestones but didn’t provide updated figures. The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting notetaking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn. “Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it — a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, partner and co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.” There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola , and Read AI ; new entrants like Calendly , Wispr , and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom ; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill. Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant , a search function that works across apps , and integration with other AI tools . Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings. “When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first 20 minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said. The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a prebrief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.
